items.question: What happens to a ray of light passing through the optical centre of a lens?
items.answer:
- It emerges without any deviation (goes straight through).
- This rule is used in drawing ray diagrams for lenses.

items.question: What happens to a ray parallel to the principal axis after passing through a convex lens?
items.answer:
- After refraction it passes through the principal focus F2 on the other side of the lens.
- (For a concave lens it appears to diverge from F1.)

items.question: State the three standard rays used to draw ray diagrams for lenses.
items.answer:
- A ray parallel to the principal axis: after refraction passes through F (convex) or appears to diverge from F (concave).
- A ray through the principal focus: after refraction emerges parallel to the principal axis.
- A ray through the optical centre: emerges without any deviation.

items.question: Using ray diagram rules, describe the image formed by a convex lens when the object is beyond 2F1.
items.answer:
- A ray parallel to the axis refracts through F2; a ray through the optical centre goes straight.
- These refracted rays meet between F2 and 2F2.
- Hence the image is formed between F2 and 2F2.
- It is diminished, real and inverted.

items.question: How does a concave lens form an image of an object at a finite distance? Explain using ray diagram rules.
items.answer:
- A ray parallel to the axis, after refraction, appears to diverge from the focus F1 on the same side.
- A ray through the optical centre goes straight without deviation.
- These two refracted rays appear to meet on the same side as the object, between F1 and O.
- The image formed is virtual, erect and diminished.

items.question: Describe the three rules used for constructing ray diagrams for lenses, mentioning the behaviour for both convex and concave lenses.
items.answer:
- Ray parallel to the principal axis: in a convex lens it refracts through the focus F2 on the far side; in a concave lens it appears to diverge from the focus F1 on the same side.
- Ray through the principal focus: in a convex lens (through F1) it emerges parallel to the axis; in a concave lens (directed towards F2) it emerges parallel to the axis.
- Ray through the optical centre: emerges without any deviation for both lenses.
- The intersection (real or apparent) of any two refracted rays gives the position of the image.
- These rules allow the nature, position and size of images to be found for any object position.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: A ray passing through the optical centre of a lens:
items.answer: B
items.explanation: A ray through the optical centre goes straight through without deviation. The other behaviours apply to other standard rays.

items.question: A ray parallel to the principal axis, after passing through a convex lens, goes through:
items.answer: B
items.explanation: For a convex lens, a parallel ray refracts through the focus F2 on the far side. The other points are incorrect.

items.question: A ray passing through the principal focus of a convex lens, after refraction, emerges:
items.answer: A
items.explanation: This is the reverse of the parallel-ray rule: a ray through F1 emerges parallel to the principal axis. The others are incorrect.

items.question: In a ray diagram, the position of the image is located at the point where:

options.B: two refracted rays intersect or appear to intersect

items.answer: B
items.explanation: The image is found where at least two refracted rays intersect (or appear to). One ray or a fixed point cannot locate it.

items.question: For a concave lens, a ray parallel to the principal axis, after refraction, appears to:

options.B: diverge from F1 on the same side

items.answer: B
items.explanation: A concave lens diverges parallel rays so that they appear to come from the focus F1 on the same side as the incoming light. It does not converge them.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: We apply the same rules for signs of distances as for spherical mirrors, except that all measurements are taken from the OPTICAL CENTRE of the lens.
According to the convention, the FOCAL LENGTH of a CONVEX lens is POSITIVE.
The FOCAL LENGTH of a CONCAVE lens is NEGATIVE.
Appropriate signs must be applied for the values of u (object distance), v (image distance), f (focal length), object height h and image height h'.

items.question: From which point are all distances measured in the sign convention for lenses?
items.answer:
- All measurements are taken from the optical centre of the lens.
- This is the main difference from the mirror convention (where distances are measured from the pole).

items.question: State the sign of the focal length of a convex lens and a concave lens, and mention the quantities to which signs must be applied.
items.answer:
- The focal length of a convex lens is positive.
- The focal length of a concave lens is negative.
- Appropriate signs must be applied to u, v, f, object height h and image height h'.

items.question: Explain the sign convention for spherical lenses.
items.answer:
- The sign convention for lenses is similar to that for spherical mirrors.
- The rules for the signs of distances are the same, but all measurements are taken from the optical centre of the lens.
- The focal length of a convex lens is taken as positive and that of a concave lens as negative.
- Care must be taken to apply correct signs to u, v, f, h and h' while solving problems.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: In the sign convention for lenses, all distances are measured from the:
items.answer: B
items.explanation: For lenses, distances are measured from the optical centre (unlike mirrors, where they are measured from the pole).

items.question: The focal length of a convex lens is taken as:
items.answer: B
items.explanation: By convention, the focal length of a convex (converging) lens is positive; that of a concave lens is negative.

items.question: The focal length of a concave lens is taken as:
items.answer: B
items.explanation: A concave (diverging) lens has a negative focal length by the sign convention. A convex lens has a positive focal length.

items.question: The sign convention for lenses is similar to that for:
items.answer: B
items.explanation: The lens sign convention follows the same rules as for spherical mirrors, except distances are measured from the optical centre.

items.question: Correct signs must be applied to which of the following while solving lens problems?

options.C: u, v, f, object height h and image height h'

items.answer: C
items.explanation: Signs must be applied to all of u, v, f, h and h' to get correct results, not just to some of them.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: LENS FORMULA: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f ... (Eq. 9.8). It is general and valid in all situations for any spherical lens, with proper signs.
MAGNIFICATION (m): m = height of the image (h') / height of the object (h) = h'/h ... (Eq. 9.9).
Magnification is also related to object distance and image distance: m = h'/h = v/u ... (Eq. 9.10).
Note: For lenses, m = v/u (positive sign), unlike mirrors where m = - v/u.
A positive magnification indicates a virtual and erect image; a negative magnification indicates a real and inverted image.
EXAMPLE 9.3:

A concave lens has focal length of 15 cm. At what distance should the object from the lens be placed so that it forms an image at 10 cm from the lens? Also, find the magnification produced by the lens.
SOLUTION:
A concave lens always forms a virtual, erect image on the same side of the object.
Image-distance v = - 10 cm; Focal length f = - 15 cm; Object-distance u = ?
Since 1/v - 1/u = 1/f
or, u = - 30 cm
Thus, the object-distance is 30 cm.
Magnification m = v/u
The positive sign shows that the image is erect and virtual. The image is one-third of the size of the object.
EXAMPLE 9.4:

A 2.0 cm tall object is placed perpendicular to the principal axis of a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. The distance of the object from the lens is 15 cm. Find the nature, position and size of the image. Also find its magnification.
SOLUTION:
Height of the object h = + 2.0 cm; Focal length f = + 10 cm; object-distance u = - 15 cm; Image-distance v = ?; Height of the image h' = ?
Since 1/v - 1/u = 1/f
or, v = + 30 cm
The positive sign of v shows that the image is formed at a distance of 30 cm on the other side of the optical centre. The image is real and inverted.
Magnification m = h'/h = v/u
or, h' = h (v/u)
Height of the image, h' = (2.0)(+30/-15) = - 4.0 cm
Magnification m = v/u

The negative signs of m and h' show that the image is inverted and real. It is formed below the principal axis. Thus, a real, inverted image, 4 cm tall, is formed at a distance of 30 cm on the other side of the lens. The image is two times enlarged.

items.question: Write the lens formula and name the quantities in it.
items.answer:
- Lens formula: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f.
- Here v = image distance, u = object distance, f = focal length, all measured from the optical centre.

items.question: Write the formula for magnification produced by a lens in terms of u and v.
items.answer:
- m = h'/h = v/u.
- Here h' is image height, h is object height.

items.question: How does the lens formula differ from the magnification formula of a mirror, and what does the sign of m indicate for a lens?
items.answer:
- The lens formula is 1/v - 1/u = 1/f (with a minus sign), while the mirror formula is 1/v + 1/u = 1/f.
- For a lens, magnification m = v/u (positive), whereas for a mirror m = - v/u.
- A positive m indicates a virtual, erect image and a negative m indicates a real, inverted image.

items.question: A concave lens of focal length 15 cm forms an image at 10 cm from the lens. Find the object distance.
items.answer:
- For a concave lens, image is virtual: v = - 10 cm, f = - 15 cm.
- 1/u = 1/v - 1/f = -1/10 + 1/15 = (-3 + 2)/30 = -1/30.
- u = - 30 cm.
- The object is placed 30 cm from the lens.

items.question: A 2.0 cm tall object is placed 15 cm from a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Find the position and size of the image.
items.answer:
- u = - 15 cm, f = + 10 cm.
- 1/v = 1/u + 1/f = -1/15 + 1/10 = (-2 + 3)/30 = 1/30, so v = + 30 cm (real image, other side).
- h' = h (v/u) = 2.0 x (30/-15) = - 4.0 cm.
- The image is real, inverted, 4 cm tall, formed 30 cm from the lens.

items.question: State the lens formula and magnification formula. Using them, find the nature, position, size and magnification of the image when a 2.0 cm object is placed 15 cm from a convex lens of focal length 10 cm.
items.answer:
- Lens formula: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f; Magnification: m = h'/h = v/u.
- Given u = - 15 cm, f = + 10 cm, h = + 2.0 cm.
- 1/v = 1/u + 1/f = -1/15 + 1/10 = 1/30, so v = + 30 cm.
- The image is real and formed 30 cm on the other side of the lens.
- m = v/u = 30/(-15) = - 2, so the image is inverted and twice enlarged.
- h' = m x h = - 2 x 2.0 = - 4.0 cm; the image is 4 cm tall, real and inverted.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: The ability of a lens to converge or diverge light rays depends on its focal length.
A convex lens of short focal length bends light rays through large angles, focussing them closer to the optical centre. A concave lens of very short focal length causes higher divergence.
POWER of a lens P = 1/f ... (Eq. 9.11), where f is the focal length.
The SI unit of power of a lens is the DIOPTRE, denoted by the letter D.
1 dioptre is the power of a lens whose focal length is 1 metre: 1D = 1 m^-1.
The power of a CONVEX lens is POSITIVE and that of a CONCAVE lens is NEGATIVE.
If f is expressed in metres, then power is expressed in dioptres.
Example: A lens of power + 2.0 D is convex with focal length + 0.50 m; a lens of power - 2.5 D is concave with focal length - 0.40 m.

sections.label: ADDITIONAL FACTS (More to Know):
sections.text:
- Many optical instruments consist of a number of lenses combined to increase the magnification and sharpness of the image.
- The net power (P) of the lenses placed in contact is given by the algebraic sum of the individual powers: P = P1 + P2 + P3 + ...
- The use of powers, instead of focal lengths, is convenient for opticians. During eye-testing, an optician puts several different combinations of corrective lenses of known power in the testing spectacles' frame; the power required is found by simple algebraic addition.
- For example, a combination of two lenses of power + 2.0 D and + 0.25 D is equivalent to a single lens of power + 2.25 D.
- This additive property is used to design lens systems (with several lenses in contact) for cameras, microscopes and telescopes, minimising defects in images.

items.question: A convex lens forms a real and inverted image of a needle at a distance of 50 cm from it. Where is the needle placed in front of the convex lens if the image is equal to the size of the object? Also, find the power of the lens.
items.answer:
Since the image is real, inverted and of the same size as the object, the object must be at 2F1 and the image at 2F2.
So image-distance v = + 50 cm and object-distance u = - 50 cm (object at 2F1 means 2f = 50 cm).
Therefore the needle is placed at 50 cm in front of the lens.
Focal length f = 50/2 = 25 cm = 0.25 m.
Power P = 1/f = 1/0.25 = + 4.0 D.

items.question: Find the power of a concave lens of focal length 2 m.
items.answer:
For a concave lens, f = - 2 m. Power P = 1/f = 1/(-2) = - 0.5 D. The negative sign confirms it is a concave (diverging) lens.

items.question: State the sign of the power for convex and concave lenses, and find the power of a convex lens of focal length 50 cm.
items.answer:
- The power of a convex lens is positive; the power of a concave lens is negative.
- For a convex lens of focal length 50 cm = 0.50 m: P = 1/f = 1/0.50 = + 2.0 D.

items.question: Two lenses of power + 2.0 D and + 0.25 D are placed in contact. Find the net power and the focal length of the combination.
items.answer:
- Net power P = P1 + P2 = + 2.0 + 0.25 = + 2.25 D.
- Focal length f = 1/P = 1/2.25 m = 0.44 m (approximately 44 cm).
- The combination acts as a single convex lens.
- The sign is positive, so the combination is converging.

items.question: Find the focal length and type of a lens of power - 2.0 D.
items.answer:
- Power P = - 2.0 D, so focal length f = 1/P = 1/(-2.0) = - 0.5 m.
- The focal length is - 50 cm.
- The negative sign shows that the lens is concave.
- Hence it is a diverging (concave) lens.

sections.label: WHAT YOU HAVE LEARNT
sections.text:
- Light seems to travel in straight lines.
- Mirrors and lenses form images of objects. Images can be either real or virtual, depending on the position of the object.
- The reflecting surfaces, of all types, obey the laws of reflection. The refracting surfaces obey the laws of refraction.
- New Cartesian Sign Conventions are followed for spherical mirrors and lenses.
- Mirror formula, 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, gives the relationship between the object-distance (u), image-distance (v), and focal length (f) of a spherical mirror.
- The focal length of a spherical mirror is equal to half its radius of curvature.
- The magnification produced by a spherical mirror is the ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object.
- A light ray travelling obliquely from a denser medium to a rarer medium bends away from the normal. A light ray bends towards the normal when it travels obliquely from a rarer to a denser medium.
- Light travels in vacuum with an enormous speed of 3 x 10^8 m/s. The speed of light is different in different media.
- The refractive index of a transparent medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to that in the medium.
- In case of a rectangular glass slab, the refraction takes place at both air-glass interface and glass-air interface. The emergent ray is parallel to the direction of the incident ray.
- Lens formula, 1/v - 1/u = 1/f, gives the relationship between the object-distance (u), image-distance (v), and the focal length (f) of a spherical lens.
- Power of a lens is the reciprocal of its focal length. The SI unit of power of a lens is dioptre.

items.question: One-half of a convex lens is covered with a black paper. Will this lens produce a complete image of the object? Verify your answer experimentally. Explain your observations.
items.answer:
- Yes, the lens will still produce a complete image of the object.
- Light passing through the uncovered half of the lens is enough to form the full image, because every part of the lens forms a complete image.
- However, the image will be less bright (dimmer) because fewer rays of light reach the lens.
- Experimentally, covering half a convex lens and forming the image of a candle on a screen still shows the complete image, only dimmer.
